questions.stem: A 74 year old man has had occasional light-headed spells for a month. He is otherwise well. His pulse rate is 58 bpm and irregular, BP 132/78 mmHg. A rhythm strip is recorded (see item resources). The PR interval gets longer with each beat until a P wave is not followed by a QRS complex, and then the cycle repeats.

visual.title: Rhythm strip
visual.caption: Progressive PR prolongation until a non-conducted P wave: Mobitz I (Wenckebach).

questions.q: Which is the most likely rhythm?
questions.e: Progressive PR lengthening until a QRS is dropped is Mobitz I (Wenckebach). Mobitz II has a constant PR with intermittent dropped QRS.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.

clues: PR interval gets longer with each beat
not followed by a QRS complex
steps.x: PR **lengthens progressively** then a beat is dropped, and it repeats.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: That is **Wenckebach: Mobitz I**.

elim: Irregularly irregular with no P waves; here P waves are present in a repeating pattern.
No relationship between P and QRS at all; here the PR lengthens predictably.
A long but constant PR with no dropped beats.
Constant PR with sudden dropped beats, not progressive lengthening.

steps.x: **D. Second-degree heart block (Mobitz I).** Lengthening PR then a dropped beat = Mobitz I; constant PR then a dropped beat = Mobitz II.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has a routine ECG before knee surgery. She has no symptoms. Her pulse rate is 64 bpm and regular, BP 126/80 mmHg. The ECG shows sinus rhythm with every P wave followed by a QRS complex. The PR interval is 260 ms on every beat and the QRS duration is 90 ms.

visual.title: Rhythm strip
visual.caption: Constant PR of 260 ms with every P wave conducted: first-degree heart block.

questions.q: Which is the most likely ECG diagnosis?
questions.e: A prolonged but constant PR interval (over 200 ms) with every P conducted is first-degree heart block. WPW causes a short PR.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.

clues: PR interval is 260 ms on every beat
every P wave followed by a QRS complex
steps.x: PR **long (260 ms) but constant**, no dropped beats.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **First-degree heart block**.

elim: P waves and QRS complexes would be dissociated.
Needs a QRS over 120 ms; hers is 90 ms.
Needs progressive PR lengthening and dropped beats.
Gives a SHORT PR (under 120 ms) with a delta wave.

steps.x: **B. First-degree heart block.** First-degree block: prolonged PR, every beat conducted.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man is admitted 2 days after an inferior myocardial infarction with dizziness. His pulse rate is 36 bpm and regular, BP 96/60 mmHg. Intermittent large waves are seen in his jugular venous pulse. A rhythm strip is recorded (see item resources). P waves at 80 per minute march through the strip with no relationship to the broad QRS complexes.

visual.title: Rhythm strip
visual.caption: Regular P waves with no relationship to slow broad QRS complexes: complete heart block.

questions.q: Which is the most likely rhythm?
questions.e: No relationship between P waves and QRS complexes, with cannon A waves from atria contracting against closed valves, is third-degree (complete) heart block.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.

clues: no relationship to the broad QRS complexes
Intermittent large waves are seen in his jugular venous pulse
steps.x: P waves and QRS **independent**; **cannon A waves** in the JVP.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Complete (third-degree) heart block**.

elim: PR lengthens then a beat drops; P and QRS remain related.
Constant PR with occasional dropped beats; P and QRS still related.
Each P would be followed by a QRS with a normal PR.
Fast broad-complex rhythm, not 36 bpm.

steps.x: **A. Complete heart block.** AV dissociation + cannon A waves = complete heart block.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman with hypertension has a 12-lead ECG for breathlessness. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and regular, BP 148/86 mmHg. The ECG shows sinus rhythm, QRS duration 150 ms, a deep dominant S wave in V1 and broad, notched M-shaped R waves in leads I, aVL and V6.
questions.q: Which is the most likely ECG diagnosis?
questions.e: Broad QRS (over 120 ms) with a dominant S wave in V1 and an M-shaped R in I, aVL and V6 is left bundle branch block.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.

clues: M-shaped R waves in leads I, aVL and V6
steps.x: Broad QRS, **dominant S in V1**, **M in the lateral leads**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **LBBB** (WiLLiaM: W in V1, M in V6).

elim: A long PR interval, not a broad QRS.
RSR' in V1 to V3 with a slurred S in I and V6, the reverse pattern.
A fast broad-complex rhythm; she is at 78 bpm in sinus rhythm.
Short PR with a delta wave.

steps.x: **B. Left bundle branch block.** LBBB: broad QRS, dominant S V1, notched M-shaped R in I/aVL/V6. RBBB is the reverse (MaRRoW).

questions.stem: A 58 year old man with COPD has an ECG at a pre-operative assessment. He is asymptomatic. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and regular, BP 130/78 mmHg. The ECG shows sinus rhythm, QRS duration 130 ms, an RSR' pattern in V1 to V3 and broad slurred S waves in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6.
questions.q: Which is the most likely ECG diagnosis?
questions.e: An RSR' (M-shaped) pattern in V1 to V3 with slurred S waves in I, aVL, V5 and V6 is right bundle branch block.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.

clues: RSR' pattern in V1 to V3
slurred S waves in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6
steps.x: Broad QRS with **RSR' in V1 to V3** and slurred lateral S waves.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **RBBB** (MaRRoW: M in V1, W in V6).

elim: Sawtooth flutter waves, not an RSR' QRS pattern.
Prolonged PR, not a broad QRS.
Dominant S in V1 and M-shaped R in the lateral leads.
Dropped beats, not a broad QRS pattern.

steps.x: **D. Right bundle branch block.** RBBB: RSR' in V1 to V3, slurred S in I/aVL/V5-6.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman with known mitral valve disease has had palpitations and breathlessness for 1 day. Her pulse rate is 150 bpm and regular, BP 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. A rhythm strip is recorded (see item resources). It shows a regular sawtooth baseline at 300 per minute, with two atrial waves for every QRS complex.

visual.title: Rhythm strip
visual.caption: Sawtooth flutter waves at 300 per minute with 2:1 conduction: atrial flutter.

questions.q: Which is the most likely rhythm?
questions.e: A regular rate of 150 bpm with sawtooth waves at 300 per minute conducted 2:1 is atrial flutter, often secondary to valvular disease such as mitral stenosis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.

clues: two atrial waves for every QRS complex
steps.x: Regular 150, **sawtooth** atrial waves at 300, **2:1** conduction, valvular disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Atrial flutter**.

elim: Irregularly irregular with no organised atrial activity.
Each QRS would follow one normal P wave.
Usually 180 to 250 bpm without sawtooth flutter waves.
Broad QRS complexes and no sawtooth atrial activity.

steps.x: **B. Atrial flutter.** Regular narrow tachycardia at 150 = think flutter with 2:1 block; look in II and V1.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man who had an anterior myocardial infarction 2 years ago has palpitations and light-headedness. He is alert. His pulse rate is 150 bpm and regular, BP 112/70 mmHg, oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. A rhythm strip is recorded (see item resources). It shows a regular broad-complex tachycardia with QRS duration 160 ms.

visual.title: Rhythm strip
visual.caption: Regular broad-complex tachycardia at 150 bpm, QRS 160 ms: ventricular tachycardia.

questions.q: Which is the most likely rhythm?
questions.e: A regular broad-complex tachycardia around 150 bpm (QRS 160 ms) after a previous MI is ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.
Previous MI, regular, **broad** (160 ms), about 150.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Ventricular tachycardia**.

elim: Irregularly irregular and usually narrow-complex.
Narrow complexes with sawtooth flutter waves.
Narrow complexes each preceded by a P wave.
No organised QRS complexes and no pulse; he is talking with a BP.

steps.x: **E. Ventricular tachycardia.** Broad-complex regular tachycardia after MI = VT until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man is on the coronary care unit after a myocardial infarction. He suddenly becomes unresponsive. He has no pulse and is not breathing. The monitor (see item resources) shows a chaotic, irregular trace of varying amplitude with no identifiable QRS complexes.

visual.title: Rhythm strip
visual.caption: Chaotic irregular deflections with no identifiable QRS complexes: ventricular fibrillation.

questions.q: Which is the most likely rhythm?
questions.e: A chaotic trace with no clear QRS complexes in a pulseless patient is ventricular fibrillation: no coordinated contraction, no output, and the commonest cause of cardiac death. It needs immediate defibrillation.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.
Pulseless, **chaotic** trace, **no QRS**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **VF**: defibrillate now.

elim: A flat line, not a chaotic trace.
Irregular QRS complexes are still seen and there is a pulse.
Slow, regular broad QRS complexes are present.
Organised broad QRS complexes twisting around the baseline.

steps.x: **E. Ventricular fibrillation.** No clear QRS + no pulse = VF, the commonest cause of cardiac death.

questions.stem: An 81 year old woman with atrial fibrillation takes digoxin and apixaban. She attends for a routine review and feels well. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and irregularly irregular, BP 132/74 mmHg. A 12-lead ECG (see item resources) shows widespread sagging, downsloping ST depression with a 'reverse tick' shape in the lateral leads.

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Irregularly irregular rhythm with widespread downsloping 'reverse tick' ST depression: digoxin effect.

questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of the ST segment changes?
questions.e: Widespread downsloping ST depression with a 'reverse tick' in a patient taking digoxin is the digoxin effect, which does not by itself mean toxicity.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.
On **digoxin**, well, with **reverse tick** ST depression.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Digoxin effect**.

elim: Would give ST elevation, and she is pain free.
Causes peaked T waves and broad QRS, not reverse-tick ST depression.
Gives a broad QRS with an M-shaped R.
Gives ST depression in V1 to V3 with tall R waves, in a patient with chest pain.

steps.x: **B. Digoxin effect.** Reverse tick ST depression = digoxin effect (not necessarily toxicity).

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has had palpitations and sweating for 2 days. His pulse rate at the wrist is 104 bpm and irregularly irregular, but the apex rate counted by auscultation is 136 bpm. His BP is 128/80 mmHg. No A wave is visible in the jugular venous pulse. ECG (see item resources) shows a narrow-complex irregular rhythm without P waves.

visual.title: Rhythm strip
visual.caption: Irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm with no P waves: atrial fibrillation.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fast AF gives an irregularly irregular pulse with an apical-radial deficit, absent P waves on the ECG and an absent A wave in the JVP (no atrial contraction).

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.

clues: apex rate counted by auscultation is 136 bpm
steps.x: Irregularly irregular, **apical-radial deficit**, **no A wave**, no P waves.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Fast **atrial fibrillation**.

elim: Regular, with sawtooth flutter waves (usually 2:1 at 150).
Ectopics occur on a sinus rhythm with visible P waves.
P waves present and the rate varies with breathing.
Regular, with sudden onset and offset.

steps.x: **A. Atrial fibrillation.** AF: irregularly irregular pulse, apex-radial deficit, no P waves, no JVP A wave.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman who grew up in Nigeria has had palpitations and breathlessness for 1 week. She had rheumatic fever as a child. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm and irregularly irregular, BP 118/74 mmHg. There is a low-pitched rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. ECG shows atrial fibrillation.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her atrial fibrillation?
questions.e: Rheumatic fever leading to mitral stenosis (mid-diastolic rumble at the apex) is a classic cause of atrial fibrillation, alongside excess alcohol.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.
Rheumatic fever + **mid-diastolic apical rumble** = mitral stenosis, now in AF.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Cause: **mitral stenosis**.

elim: Gives an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids.
Gives an ejection systolic murmur that increases with Valsalva.
Gives a mid-systolic click and late systolic murmur.
No murmur and no rheumatic history; a less likely cause here.

steps.x: **C. Mitral stenosis.** AF classic links: rheumatic fever / mitral stenosis and alcohol.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman with depression takes citalopram 40 mg daily. She had a brief faint at work. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and regular, BP 122/76 mmHg. Her 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm. The QT interval, measured from the start of the Q wave to the end of the T wave and corrected for rate, is 492 ms.
questions.q: Which is the most likely ECG diagnosis?
questions.e: A QTc above 460 ms in a woman (440 ms in a man) is prolonged. Citalopram is a recognised cause, raising the risk of torsades de pointes.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.
On **citalopram**, a faint, QTc **492 ms** in a woman.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Above 460 ms: **long QT**.

elim: Defined by a long PR, not a long QT.
A broad QRS, not a long QT.
The upper limit for a woman is 460 ms; 492 ms is prolonged.
Short PR with a delta wave.

steps.x: **D. Prolonged QT interval.** Long QT: QTc over 460 ms (women) or 440 ms (men); SSRIs and macrolides prolong it.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has palpitations that began 3 hours ago. His pulse rate is 168 bpm and regular. He fainted in the waiting room and is now pale and sweaty. His BP is 82/54 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. ECG shows a narrow-complex regular tachycardia.
questions.q: Which feature most clearly mandates immediate synchronised DC cardioversion?
questions.e: Adverse features (shock, syncope, heart failure, myocardial ischaemia, chest pain) in a tachyarrhythmia mandate urgent synchronised DC cardioversion.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.

clues: He fainted in the waiting room
steps.x: Tachyarrhythmia with **syncope** and **shock** (BP 82/54).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Adverse features = **synchronised DC cardioversion**.

elim: Age is not an adverse feature.
QRS width does not decide the need for cardioversion; adverse features do.
Acceptable saturation.
Duration is not an adverse feature.

steps.x: **E. Syncope with hypotension.** Adverse features: shock, syncope, heart failure, chest pain or ischaemia = cardiovert.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman has had dizzy spells for a week. Her pulse rate is 48 bpm, BP 118/70 mmHg. She is alert with no chest pain or breathlessness. Atropine is being drawn up. Her continuous monitoring shows sinus bradycardia with one recorded ventricular pause of 3.6 seconds.
questions.q: Which feature of her presentation most indicates a risk of asystole?
questions.e: Risk factors for asystole in bradycardia are complete heart block with broad QRS, recent asystole, Mobitz II and a ventricular pause over 3 seconds.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.
A pause **over 3 seconds** is recorded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: That is an **asystole risk factor**.

elim: Age is not an asystole risk factor in the bradycardia algorithm.
Reassuring, not a risk factor.
A normal BP is reassuring.
Bradycardia alone is not a listed asystole risk; the long pause is.

steps.x: **E. Ventricular pause of 3.6 seconds.** Asystole risk: CHB with broad QRS, recent asystole, Mobitz II, pause over 3 seconds.

questions.stem: An 82 year old woman has had recurrent dizzy spells and one fall. A 24-hour tape shows periods of sinus bradycardia at 38 bpm, sinus pauses of 2.5 seconds, and runs of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation at 140 bpm. She takes no rate-limiting drugs. Her electrolytes and thyroid function are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Alternating sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses and paroxysmal tachycardia (tachy-brady) in an older patient is sick sinus syndrome, one of the main causes of bradyarrhythmia with heart block.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.
Brady (under 60) and tachy (over 100) alternating, with **sinus pauses**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Tachy-brady: **sick sinus syndrome**.

elim: P waves and QRS dissociated; here the problem is sinus node pauses.
A long PR only; no pauses or tachycardia.
Dropped QRS after a conducted P, not sinus pauses with tachy runs.
Short PR and delta wave in younger patients.

steps.x: **D. Sick sinus syndrome.** Bradyarrhythmias come from heart block or sick sinus syndrome (tachy-brady).

questions.stem: A 41 year old man has palpitations that began suddenly while lifting boxes 40 minutes ago. He has had similar episodes that stop abruptly. He feels light-headed but has no chest pain. His pulse rate is 196 bpm and regular, BP 124/80 mmHg. A rhythm strip (see item resources) shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia with no visible P waves.

visual.title: Rhythm strip
visual.caption: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 196 bpm with no visible P waves: SVT.

questions.q: Which is the most likely rhythm?
questions.e: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia around 200 bpm with abrupt onset and offset is SVT (usually AVNRT).

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.
**Sudden** onset and offset, regular, narrow, about 200.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Irregularly irregular.
Usually regular at 150 with sawtooth waves.
Gradual onset with visible P waves, rarely 196 bpm at rest.
Broad QRS complexes.

steps.x: **D. Supraventricular tachycardia.** Sudden on, sudden off, regular narrow complex = SVT.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with heart failure takes furosemide 80 mg daily. He has had palpitations and muscle weakness for 3 days. His pulse rate is 110 bpm and irregular, BP 118/72 mmHg. ECG shows frequent ventricular ectopics, flattened T waves and prominent U waves.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his arrhythmia?
questions.e: Loop diuretics cause hypokalaemia, an electrolyte cause of arrhythmia, with flat T waves and U waves on the ECG.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.

clues: flattened T waves and prominent U waves
steps.x: On a **loop diuretic**, weak, **U waves** and flat T waves, potassium 2.7.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Electrolyte cause: **hypokalaemia**.

elim: Causes a short QT, not U waves; calcium is not low.
Causes peaked T waves; his potassium is low.
Rare and causes bradycardia, not this pattern.
Causes confusion, not U waves and ectopics.

steps.x: **D. Hypokalaemia.** Causes of arrhythmia: ischaemia, electrolytes (K+), drugs, structural disease.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman comes to the Emergency Department with palpitations that started 1 hour ago and are still present. She has no chest pain. Her pulse rate is 140 bpm and irregular, BP 130/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: The 12-lead ECG is the gold standard: it captures the rhythm and morphology while the arrhythmia is ongoing.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide which test answers the exact question asked (initial or diagnostic).
The arrhythmia is **happening now**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Capture it: **12-lead ECG**.

elim: For recurrent episodes not captured; hers is ongoing now.
Does not identify the rhythm.
Looks for structural causes after the rhythm is known.
Assesses myocardial injury, not the rhythm.

steps.x: **A. 12-lead ECG.** Ongoing palpitations = 12-lead ECG first (gold standard).

questions.stem: A 60 year old man has an ECG which a junior doctor thinks shows first-degree heart block. The registrar asks how the interval used to make this diagnosis should be measured. His pulse rate is 66 bpm and regular, BP 134/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the correct way to measure this interval?
o: End of the P wave to the start of the QRS
Peak of the P wave to the peak of the R wave
Start of the P wave to the start of the QRS
Start of the Q wave to the end of the T wave
Start of the QRS to the end of the QRS
questions.e: First-degree heart block is a prolonged PR interval, measured from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS complex (normal 120 to 200 ms).

steps.x: An investigation question: decide which test answers the exact question asked (initial or diagnostic).

clues: how the interval used to make this diagnosis should be measured
steps.x: First-degree block is defined by the **PR interval**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: PR = **start of P to start of QRS**.

elim: That is the PR segment, not the PR interval.
Not a standard interval.
That is the QT interval.
That is the QRS duration.

steps.x: **C. Start of the P wave to the start of the QRS.** PR interval: start of P to start of QRS; QT: start of Q to end of T.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman is found to be in new atrial fibrillation at a GP visit. A 12-lead ECG confirms AF at 96 bpm. She has had weight loss and heat intolerance. Her BP is 136/80 mmHg. The GP wants to look for an underlying cause.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: After the ECG, bloods (thyroid function, electrolytes) and an echocardiogram look for a cause such as thyrotoxicosis, electrolyte imbalance or structural heart disease.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide which test answers the exact question asked (initial or diagnostic).
Rhythm already confirmed; now find the **cause** (she sounds thyrotoxic).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bloods (TFTs, U&E) and echo**.

elim: The rhythm is already captured.
Not a first-line test for the cause of AF.
No features of PE.
Not used to find the cause of AF.

steps.x: **E. Thyroid function, electrolytes and echocardiogram.** New arrhythmia: ECG, then bloods and echo for the cause.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man has had three unexplained collapses over 6 weeks, each with brief loss of consciousness and rapid recovery. Between episodes he is well. His pulse rate is 64 bpm and regular, BP 138/80 mmHg with no postural drop. A 12-lead ECG and blood tests are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Recurrent uncaptured collapse with a normal resting ECG needs ambulatory monitoring with a 24-hour Holter to catch the arrhythmia.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide which test answers the exact question asked (initial or diagnostic).

clues: A 12-lead ECG and blood tests are normal
steps.x: Recurrent collapse, **normal resting ECG**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Catch the arrhythmia: **24-hour Holter**.

elim: Rapid recovery without neurological signs points to a cardiac rhythm cause.
No features of seizures.
Already normal; it only captures a few seconds.
For reflex syncope; no postural drop and no prodrome described.

steps.x: **A. 24-hour Holter monitor.** Recurrent uncaptured arrhythmia or collapse = Holter monitor.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man is found to have atrial fibrillation. He has hypertension treated with amlodipine. He has no diabetes, heart failure, vascular disease or previous stroke. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and irregularly irregular, BP 138/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is his CHA2DS2-VASc score?
questions.e: Age 65 to 74 (1) plus hypertension (1) gives a CHA2DS2-VASc of 2; male sex scores 0. A man scoring 1 or more should be considered for anticoagulation.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide which test answers the exact question asked (initial or diagnostic).

clues: no diabetes, heart failure, vascular disease or previous stroke
steps.x: Age 67 = 1, hypertension = 1, male = 0.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **2**: above the male threshold of 1, so anticoagulate.

elim: He scores for both age and hypertension.
Counts only one of age 65 to 74 and hypertension.
Would need another factor such as diabetes.
Overcounts; male sex scores nothing.

steps.x: **C. 2.** CHA2DS2-VASc: CCF, HTN, age 65-74, DM, vascular, female = 1 each; age 75+ or stroke = 2.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man with atrial fibrillation is about to start apixaban. His haemoglobin is 124 g/L, eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73m² and he had a gastrointestinal bleed 3 years ago. His BP is 132/78 mmHg. The doctor wants a formal assessment of his bleeding risk on anticoagulation, as recommended by NICE.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate tool?
questions.e: NICE (2021) recommends the ORBIT score for bleeding risk on anticoagulation: age 75+, anaemia, bleeding history, reduced eGFR and antiplatelet use.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide which test answers the exact question asked (initial or diagnostic).
Asked about **bleeding** risk; he has age, anaemia, eGFR and a bleed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: NICE 2021: **ORBIT**.

elim: Assesses stroke risk, not bleeding risk.
Pneumonia severity.
Risk in acute coronary syndrome.
Probability of DVT or PE.

steps.x: **D. ORBIT score.** Stroke risk = CHA2DS2-VASc; bleeding risk = ORBIT (NICE 2021).

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman has had palpitations for a week. She has no chest pain, breathlessness or syncope. Her pulse rate is 122 bpm and irregularly irregular, BP 138/86 mmHg. ECG confirms atrial fibrillation. She has no history of asthma. Her echocardiogram is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management of her heart rate?
questions.e: Stable AF is rate controlled first-line with a beta-blocker such as bisoprolol (or a rate-limiting calcium channel blocker); digoxin is second-line.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.

clues: no chest pain, breathlessness or syncope
steps.x: Stable AF, no adverse features, no asthma.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: First-line rate control: **bisoprolol**.

elim: Rhythm control for selected patients (heart failure, first onset, reversible cause), not first-line rate control.
For bradycardia.
Second-line rate control.
For SVT, not AF.

steps.x: **C. Bisoprolol.** AF = rate control (bisoprolol or diltiazem/verapamil); SVT = adenosine; bradycardia = atropine; VT = amiodarone.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has had regular palpitations for 25 minutes. They started suddenly. She has no chest pain or breathlessness. Her pulse rate is 184 bpm and regular, BP 120/78 mmHg, oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Stable SVT is treated first with vagal manoeuvres (Valsalva, carotid sinus massage), then IV adenosine if they fail.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.
Stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia: **SVT**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: First step: **vagal manoeuvres**.

elim: Second-line if vagal manoeuvres fail.
For VT or rhythm control, not first-line SVT.
Rate control for AF or flutter.
Only with adverse features; she is stable.

steps.x: **E. Vagal manoeuvres.** SVT ladder: vagal manoeuvres, then adenosine 6 mg, then verapamil; cardiovert if unstable.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man with severe asthma has a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 190 bpm. A modified Valsalva manoeuvre has failed twice. He has no chest pain and is alert. His BP is 122/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: If vagal manoeuvres fail in SVT, IV adenosine is given, but in asthma IV verapamil is used instead because adenosine can cause bronchospasm.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.
SVT, vagal failed, but **severe asthma**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Skip adenosine: **IV verapamil**.

elim: Avoided in asthma because it can cause bronchospasm.
Not the next step for stable SVT.
For bradycardia.
Only with adverse features.

steps.x: **D. IV verapamil.** SVT after vagal: adenosine 6 mg, or verapamil if asthmatic.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man has a heart rate of 34 bpm with dizziness and a BP of 78/50 mmHg. He has received IV atropine 500 micrograms six times (3 mg total) with no response. Transcutaneous pacing is not immediately available. His ECG shows sinus bradycardia.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Bradycardia with adverse features is treated with IV atropine 500 micrograms up to 3 mg; if it fails, an isoprenaline or adrenaline infusion is used (or pacing).

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.

clues: six times (3 mg total) with no response
steps.x: Unstable bradycardia, **atropine maxed at 3 mg**, no pacing yet.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Next drug: **adrenaline (or isoprenaline) infusion**.

elim: The maximum of 3 mg has been reached.
Slows conduction further; for SVT.
For tachyarrhythmias.
Would slow the heart further.

steps.x: **A. Adrenaline infusion.** Bradycardia: atropine 500 micrograms to 3 mg, then adrenaline/isoprenaline infusion or pacing.

questions.stem: An 80 year old woman has complete heart block with broad QRS complexes and a rate of 30 bpm. She is drowsy and her BP is 72/44 mmHg. She has not responded to atropine 3 mg or an adrenaline infusion. A permanent pacemaker cannot be placed until tomorrow.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Heart block not responding to drugs is treated with temporary pacing (transcutaneous, then transvenous) as a bridge to a permanent pacemaker.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.

clues: complete heart block with broad QRS
not responded to atropine 3 mg or an adrenaline infusion
steps.x: Unstable CHB, **drugs have failed**, PPM tomorrow.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Bridge with **temporary transcutaneous pacing**.

elim: Worsens AV block.
For tachyarrhythmias; may worsen block.
For torsades de pointes.
For tachyarrhythmias, not bradycardia.

steps.x: **E. Temporary transcutaneous pacing.** Drug-resistant heart block: transcutaneous then transvenous pacing, then PPM.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman is brought in 2 hours after taking 40 tablets of bisoprolol 10 mg. Her pulse rate is 38 bpm, BP 76/44 mmHg. She has had atropine 3 mg with little effect. Her capillary glucose is 3.6 mmol/L. ECG shows sinus bradycardia.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate specific treatment?
questions.e: Glucagon is the specific treatment for beta-blocker overdose bradycardia: it raises cAMP independently of beta-receptors.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.
**Beta-blocker overdose** with bradycardia not responding to atropine.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Specific antidote: **glucagon**.

elim: Slows AV conduction further.
Reverses benzodiazepines.
Reverses opioids.
Too late at 2 hours to treat established shock alone.

steps.x: **C. IV glucagon.** Beta-blocker overdose bradycardia = glucagon.

questions.stem: An 84 year old woman with permanent atrial fibrillation lives alone and is largely sedentary. She takes bisoprolol 10 mg daily and apixaban. Her resting pulse rate remains 112 bpm and irregularly irregular, BP 132/76 mmHg. She has no heart failure. Diltiazem caused ankle oedema.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: If first-line rate control (beta-blocker or calcium channel blocker) is insufficient, digoxin is the second-line rate control drug, especially in sedentary patients.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.
Rate still high on maximal **bisoprolol**, diltiazem not tolerated, sedentary.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Second-line rate control: **digoxin**.

elim: Used for SVT, not AF rate control.
A last resort for refractory recurrent AF.
Anticoagulation is still needed.
She is stable and in permanent AF.

steps.x: **A. Add digoxin.** AF rate control: beta-blocker or CCB first, digoxin second.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man has recurrent episodes of fast palpitations. His resting ECG shows a short PR interval of 100 ms and a slurred upstroke to the QRS complex. Between episodes he is well. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. He wants a long-term solution.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Radiofrequency ablation of the accessory pathway
questions.e: WPW (short PR, delta wave, accessory pathway: bundle of Kent) is treated first-line with radiofrequency ablation of the accessory pathway; oral sotalol is second-line.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.
Short PR and **delta wave**: WPW with an accessory pathway.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Definitive: **ablate the pathway**.

elim: Can speed conduction down the accessory pathway; avoided.
AV nodal blockers can be dangerous in WPW.
Second-line, if ablation is refused.
For bradyarrhythmias, not WPW.

steps.x: **E. Radiofrequency ablation of the accessory pathway.** WPW: radiofrequency ablation first-line; sotalol if refused.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man has had two blackouts. His ECG shows complete heart block with a ventricular rate of 34 bpm and broad QRS complexes. He was stabilised with transcutaneous pacing in the Emergency Department. There is no reversible cause: he takes no rate-limiting drugs and his electrolytes are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: Unstable complete heart block without a reversible cause needs a permanent pacemaker.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.
Symptomatic CHB, **no reversible cause**, temporarily paced.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Definitive: **permanent pacemaker**.

elim: Treats VT/VF; does not pace a bradycardia long term as its main role.
Would worsen the block.
Used for tachyarrhythmias such as AF or WPW.
A short-term measure only.

steps.x: **C. Permanent pacemaker.** Unstable CHB = permanent pacemaker.

questions.stem: A 59 year old taxi driver survived a cardiac arrest from ventricular tachycardia 1 week ago. Echocardiogram shows an old anterior infarct with an ejection fraction of 30%. Coronary angiography shows no new lesion. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. He has an ICD fitted and asks about driving his own car.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice about driving his car?
questions.e: VT survivors receive an ICD to prevent future events. After an ICD for secondary prevention he must avoid driving for 6 months.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.

clues: survived a cardiac arrest from ventricular tachycardia
steps.x: VT arrest survivor: **ICD for secondary prevention**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Driving: **stop for 6 months**.

elim: Too short for a secondary-prevention ICD.
Too short for an ICD fitted for secondary prevention.
Not permitted after an ICD for secondary prevention.
Car driving can resume after 6 months if there are no shocks.

steps.x: **C. Do not drive for 6 months.** VT = ICD to prevent future events; secondary-prevention ICD = no driving for 6 months.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman with hypertension had recurrent symptomatic atrial fibrillation despite rate and rhythm control drugs, so she underwent radiofrequency ablation 3 months ago. She is now in sinus rhythm. Her CHA2DS2-VASc score is 3. She asks to stop her apixaban because her rhythm is now normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Stop apixaban if a Holter is normal
questions.e: Radiofrequency ablation is a last resort for refractory AF and patients still need long-term anticoagulation according to their CHA2DS2-VASc score (here 3), because left atrial appendage thrombus risk persists.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.
Post-ablation, sinus rhythm, but **CHA2DS2-VASc 3**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Anticoagulation depends on the score: **continue apixaban**.

elim: Anticoagulation is guided by CHA2DS2-VASc, not the rhythm.
Ablation does not remove the stroke risk; anticoagulation follows CHA2DS2-VASc.
Aspirin is not used for stroke prevention in AF.
Antiplatelets do not prevent AF stroke.

steps.x: **A. Continue apixaban long term.** After AF ablation, anticoagulate according to CHA2DS2-VASc, not the rhythm.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has palpitations. His pulse rate is 160 bpm and regular. He is alert with no chest pain, breathlessness or syncope. His BP is 128/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. A 12-lead ECG shows a regular broad-complex tachycardia, QRS 160 ms, which is ventricular tachycardia.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: IV amiodarone 300 mg over 20 to 60 minutes
questions.e: Stable VT is treated with IV amiodarone 300 mg over 20 to 60 minutes then 900 mg over 24 hours. Unstable VT is cardioverted. Verapamil is contraindicated.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.

clues: no chest pain, breathlessness or syncope
steps.x: VT but **no adverse features**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Stable VT: **IV amiodarone 300 mg**.

elim: For SVT; not used for VT.
For bradycardia.
Contraindicated in VT; can cause haemodynamic collapse.
For unstable VT with adverse features; he is stable.

steps.x: **B. IV amiodarone 300 mg over 20 to 60 minutes.** Stable VT = amiodarone 300 mg IV; unstable VT = DC cardioversion.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman is treated with azithromycin for pneumonia. On day 2 she has a brief collapse on the ward. Her monitor shows runs of polymorphic broad-complex tachycardia whose axis twists around the baseline. Between runs her pulse rate is 64 bpm, BP 112/68 mmHg, and her QTc is 520 ms.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Torsades de pointes, precipitated by a macrolide such as azithromycin, is treated with IV magnesium sulphate 2 g, which stabilises the membrane and suppresses afterdepolarisations.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.
Macrolide, long QT, **polymorphic twisting VT**: torsades de pointes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Treat with **IV magnesium sulphate 2 g**.

elim: For SVT.
Prolongs the QT further and can worsen torsades.
For SVT; not for torsades.
Not the acute treatment.

steps.x: **C. IV magnesium sulphate 2 g.** Torsades (macrolides, hypothermia, long QT) = IV magnesium 2 g.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man has had persistent atrial fibrillation for 4 months. He is symptomatic despite rate control and an elective cardioversion is planned. He is not yet anticoagulated. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and irregularly irregular, BP 132/80 mmHg. He has no adverse features.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan?
o: Anticoagulate for 3 weeks before and 4 weeks after
questions.e: For elective cardioversion of AF lasting over 48 hours, anticoagulate for 3 weeks before and 4 weeks after. Immediate cardioversion is reserved for onset within 48 hours or instability.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.
AF for **months**, elective cardioversion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **3 weeks before, 4 weeks after**.

elim: Too short; thrombus may be present.
Pre-cardioversion anticoagulation is needed when AF has lasted over 48 hours.
AF for 4 months risks embolising atrial thrombus.
Cardioversion of long-standing AF carries stroke risk.

steps.x: **B. Anticoagulate for 3 weeks before and 4 weeks after.** Elective AF cardioversion: anticoagulate 3 weeks before and 4 weeks after; synchronise to the R wave.

questions.stem: A 75 year old woman has an acute ischaemic stroke with left-sided weakness. She is found to be in atrial fibrillation, which is thought to have caused the stroke. CT shows a moderate infarct with no haemorrhage. She is outside the thrombolysis window. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and irregularly irregular, BP 150/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Aspirin 300 mg daily for 2 weeks, then lifelong anticoagulation
questions.e: When AF has caused an ischaemic stroke, give aspirin 300 mg daily for 2 weeks, then start lifelong anticoagulation.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.

clues: thought to have caused the stroke
steps.x: Ischaemic stroke caused by AF.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Aspirin 300 mg for 2 weeks, then anticoagulate** for life.

elim: Anticoagulation is delayed for 2 weeks after an ischaemic stroke because of haemorrhagic transformation risk.
AF needs anticoagulation long term.
She needs antiplatelet then anticoagulant cover.
Anticoagulation is delayed for 2 weeks.

steps.x: **B. Aspirin 300 mg daily for 2 weeks, then lifelong anticoagulation.** AF stroke: aspirin 300 mg for 2 weeks, then lifelong anticoagulation.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 210 bpm. She has central chest pain and is clammy. Her BP is 76/48 mmHg and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. ECG shows SVT with widespread ST depression. A Valsalva manoeuvre has not helped.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: SVT with adverse features (shock, chest pain, myocardial ischaemia) needs urgent synchronised DC cardioversion, up to 3 shocks.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.
SVT with **shock** and **ischaemia**: adverse features.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Synchronised DC cardioversion** now.

elim: Appropriate in stable SVT, but she has adverse features.
Given after failed shocks, not first.
A negative inotrope; dangerous in shock.
Too slow and unsafe in shock.

steps.x: **E. Synchronised DC cardioversion.** Any tachyarrhythmia with adverse features = synchronised DC cardioversion (up to 3 shocks).

questions.stem: A 78 year old man has had palpitations for 6 hours. He is breathless with bibasal crackles and his BP is 70/50 mmHg. His pulse rate is 168 bpm and irregularly irregular. ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a fast ventricular rate. A senior is present and sedation is available.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Synchronised DC cardioversion up to 3 shocks
questions.e: Fast AF with adverse features (shock, BP 70/50, and heart failure) needs urgent synchronised DC cardioversion, up to 3 shocks.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.
Fast AF with **shock** and **heart failure**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Synchronised DC cardioversion**, up to 3 shocks.

elim: Too slow when he is in shock.
Does not treat the unstable rhythm.
Too slow and negatively inotropic in shock with heart failure.
For pulseless VF/VT; a shock must be synchronised to the R wave when there is a pulse.

steps.x: **D. Synchronised DC cardioversion up to 3 shocks.** Unstable tachyarrhythmia = synchronised DC cardioversion, up to 3 shocks, then amiodarone.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman has recurrent episodes of sudden regular palpitations at 190 bpm that stop with a Valsalva manoeuvre. Electrophysiology studies show two pathways within the AV node, a fast one and a slow one. Her resting ECG is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her tachycardia?
o: Accessory pathway causing a delta wave
Re-entry circuit within the AV node
questions.e: Most tachyarrhythmias arise from abnormal automaticity or re-entry. AVNRT is a re-entry circuit using fast and slow pathways in the AV node.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the stem.

clues: two pathways within the AV node
steps.x: Dual AV nodal pathways, terminated by vagal manoeuvre.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Re-entry within the AV node** (AVNRT).

elim: That is WPW; her resting ECG is normal.
That is AF, which is irregular.
The trigger for torsades de pointes.
Causes bradycardia (sick sinus).

steps.x: **E. Re-entry circuit within the AV node.** Tachyarrhythmias: abnormal automaticity or re-entry (AVNRT, flutter).

questions.stem: A 73 year old man has atrial fibrillation. A medical student examining his ECG notices that there are no P waves and that the RR intervals are completely irregular. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the best explanation for these ECG findings?
o: Chaotic atrial activity with unpredictable AV nodal conduction
Complete block at the AV node
Single macro re-entry circuit in the right atrium
questions.e: In AF, chaotic re-entrant atrial activity prevents coordinated contraction so no P waves form, and the AV node conducts impulses unpredictably, giving an irregularly irregular ventricular response.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the stem.
No P waves and **irregularly irregular** RR.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Chaotic atria** (no P) + **unpredictable AV node** conduction (irregular).

elim: Would give a regular slow escape rhythm.
That is WPW, with a delta wave.
Would give broad complexes.
That is flutter, which gives regular sawtooth waves.

steps.x: **A. Chaotic atrial activity with unpredictable AV nodal conduction.** AF: chaotic atria = no P waves; random AV conduction = irregularly irregular.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man had first-degree heart block on an ECG 2 years ago. Last year he developed Mobitz I and he now has complete heart block. His cardiologist explains what this progression means.
questions.q: Which is the best explanation of the progression?
o: Increasing automaticity of the sinus node
Worsening conduction at or below the AV node
questions.e: Heart block reflects impaired conduction at or below the AV node; its degree reflects severity: PR prolongation, then dropped beats, then complete AV dissociation.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the stem.
First-degree, then Mobitz I, then complete block.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Progressively **worse AV nodal conduction**.

elim: WPW: short PR, faster conduction.
Causes atrial tachyarrhythmias, not heart block.
Would cause sinus tachycardia.
Long QT, not heart block.

steps.x: **E. Worsening conduction at or below the AV node.** Heart block degree = severity of AV conduction failure: long PR, dropped beats, dissociation.

questions.stem: A 56 year old woman with long QT has torsades de pointes after starting clarithromycin. She is given IV magnesium sulphate 2 g and the arrhythmia stops. A student asks how the magnesium worked. Her QTc is 530 ms.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of action of magnesium here?
o: Increased vagal tone at the AV node
questions.e: QT prolongation reflects delayed repolarisation, which allows early afterdepolarisations to trigger torsades. Magnesium stabilises the cardiac membrane and suppresses these afterdepolarisations.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the stem.
Long QT torsades stopped by **magnesium**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Magnesium **suppresses early afterdepolarisations**.

elim: That is a beta-blocker.
Describes vagal manoeuvres or digoxin.
Irrelevant to torsades.
That is how adenosine works in SVT.

steps.x: **D. Suppression of early afterdepolarisations.** Long QT = delayed repolarisation = EADs = torsades; magnesium stabilises the membrane.
